item.title: Your Power Bill Is Now Partly an AI Bill: Inside the Auction That Prices America's Data Center Boom
item.body:
Most people will never read a capacity auction report. But if you live in one of the 13 states or the District of Columbia served by the PJM Interconnection — roughly 65 million people, from Chicago to Newark to Richmond — one line in that report has more influence over your next electricity bill than almost anything happening in your own house.

That line is the clearing price. For the delivery year that runs June 1, 2026 through May 31, 2027, it came in at **$329.17 per megawatt-day** — the effective ceiling allowed in the auction. Two delivery years earlier, the comparable price was **$28.92**.

That is not a typo, and it is not inflation. It is the price of promising that the lights stay on in a grid where demand has started growing again after roughly two decades of sitting flat — and where the fastest-growing single category of new demand is the data center.

## The three numbers that tell the story

| Delivery year | RTO-wide clearing price | Approximate total capacity cost |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 / 2025 | $28.92 per MW-day | ~$2.2 billion |
| 2025 / 2026 | $269.92 per MW-day | ~$14.7 billion |
| 2026 / 2027 | $329.17 per MW-day (at the cap) | ~$16.1 billion |

The 2026/27 auction, whose results PJM published in late July 2025, secured roughly 134,300 megawatts of capacity — a reserve margin somewhere near 19%, comfortably above the target. In other words, the system did not come up short. It simply became far more expensive to keep it that way.

## What a capacity auction actually is

This is the part that gets skipped, and it is the part that matters.

Electricity markets pay for two different things. One is **energy** — the actual kilowatt-hours you use, priced more or less continuously. The other is **capacity** — a standing commitment from a power plant, a demand-response aggregator, or a battery to be available and deliver during the worst hours of the year: the January morning when everything is frozen, the July afternoon when everything is running.

PJM buys that commitment years ahead through the Base Residual Auction. Suppliers offer to be available; PJM buys until it has enough to meet a reliability requirement; and — this is the crucial mechanic — **every cleared supplier gets paid the same clearing price**, set by the most expensive offer needed to fill the requirement. Not their own asking price. The market price.

That single design choice is why the number moves so violently. When the requirement rises past the cheap, already-built supply and starts reaching into the expensive tail of the offer stack, the price for *everything* resets upward at once. A modest increase in demand can produce a very immodest increase in cost.

Then the cost gets spread. Utilities buy capacity on behalf of their customers and pass the charge through — showing up in the supply or generation portion of your bill, in your state's price-to-compare, or in a competitive supplier's rate. You never see a line item called "capacity auction." You just see a bigger number.

## Why the price hit the ceiling

Three pressures arrived at the same time.

**Supply left.** Coal and older oil- and gas-fired units have been retiring on economics, age, and environmental compliance schedules. Once a plant deactivates, its capacity stops showing up in the auction.

**Replacement is slow.** New solar, wind, storage, and gas projects have to clear interconnection studies, permitting, local approval, financing, and equipment orders. PJM's queue holds a very large volume of proposed projects; the constraint is not developer interest but the pace of study, construction, and delivery. Heavy-duty gas turbines in particular are effectively sold out well into the next decade, with order backlogs at the handful of firms that build them.

**Demand turned upward.** After years of flat load, PJM's forecasts now show substantial peak growth through 2030 — the sharpest revision the region has seen in a generation. Electrification contributes. Manufacturing contributes. But the category driving the revision is large data-center load, concentrated heavily in Northern Virginia and spreading into Ohio, Pennsylvania, Indiana, and Maryland.

Retirements plus slow replacement plus rising demand equals a tighter requirement met by a more expensive offer stack. The auction did what it was designed to do: it printed a very loud price signal.

## How much of this is really AI?

Here the honest answer requires care, because this is where public discussion tends to get sloppy.

PJM's independent market monitor, which analyzes the auction separately from PJM itself, has published assessments attributing the large majority of the recent price increases to growth in large load — data centers above all. Under that analysis, if data-center demand growth were removed from the reliability requirement, the clearing price would be dramatically lower. That is a modeled counterfactual, not a measurement, and reasonable analysts dispute the exact share. But the direction is not seriously contested: data centers are the dominant swing factor.

Two fair counterpoints belong alongside it.

First, data centers do pay. They pay retail tariffs, they pay capacity charges proportional to their contribution to peak, and in many cases they pay for interconnection upgrades directly. They are not receiving free electricity.

Second, the grievance is about **allocation and risk**, not theft. When a uniform clearing price resets because one customer class is adding gigawatts, every other customer — the household, the school district, the machine shop — pays the new price on their existing consumption too. The build-out's cost is socialized across the whole footprint, while the revenue from the build-out is not. That asymmetry, rather than any single company's behavior, is the actual policy problem.

## What this looks like on your bill

PJM's own estimate for the 2026/27 result was an increase in the range of roughly **1.5% to 5% on typical residential bills**, varying by zone — layered on top of the considerably larger increase already working its way through from the prior auction.

Several things make the lived experience messier than that range suggests:

- **Timing varies.** States and utilities procure default supply on different cycles, so the same auction lands in different months and different chunks depending on where you live.
- **Zones differ.** Transmission constraints mean some areas clear above the RTO-wide price, and those customers absorb more.
- **Capacity is only part of the bill.** Transmission investment, distribution rates, and fuel costs move on their own schedules and can pull the total in the same direction at the same time.

If you want your actual number rather than an average, the practical path is your utility's rate filing or price-to-compare notice at your state public utility commission — that document shows the supply cost being passed through, in your zone, for your service class.

## Who is trying to fix it, and how

The response has been unusually fast by energy-regulation standards.

**A price collar.** After Pennsylvania's governor challenged the auction rules at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, PJM and the state reached a settlement that FERC approved: a floor and a ceiling on the clearing price for the 2026/27 and 2027/28 auctions. The ceiling is precisely why 2026/27 stopped at $329.17. Absent that cap, the price would very likely have gone higher — a detail worth remembering when reading the number.

**Faster interconnection for what's needed.** PJM created a fast-track pathway to move a limited slate of projects that add reliable capacity quickly, alongside broader reforms to its interconnection process.

**Making large loads carry their own weight.** This is the most consequential front. Regulators and utilities across the footprint are reworking how very large customers are treated: minimum-demand contracts so a data center pays for most of the capacity it reserves whether or not it uses it, separate rate classes for large loads, collateral and exit provisions, and rules for "bring your own generation" or co-located supply arrangements. Ohio approved a large-load framework along these lines, and similar proceedings have opened elsewhere. FERC has taken up the co-location question for PJM specifically.

**Demand flexibility.** Because the requirement is driven by a handful of peak hours, a data center willing to curtail or shift to on-site generation during those hours reduces the requirement itself. Several operators have signaled willingness; turning that into enforceable, verifiable commitments is the unfinished work.

## What to watch next

- **Subsequent auction results.** Each new Base Residual Auction tests whether new supply and demand-side commitments are arriving fast enough to pull the price off the ceiling — and what happens when the collar's coverage ends.
- **Whether large-load tariffs actually bind.** A rate class only shifts cost if its minimum-take and collateral terms survive negotiation and litigation intact.
- **Real megawatts, not announcements.** Announced generation projects are cheap; steel in the ground and turbines delivered are what changes an auction outcome.
- **Whether load forecasts hold.** Some share of the interconnection requests in the pipeline is speculative or duplicated across utilities. If forecast demand is revised down, the requirement — and the price — follows.
- **Political durability.** Rate increases of this size tend to outlast the technical debate. Legislative intervention in individual states is a live possibility.

## The bottom line

The AI build-out has a price, and part of it is being paid through an obscure auction that most ratepayers have never heard of. There is nothing hidden or improper about the mechanism — the rules are public, the results are published, and the market is doing exactly what a uniform-clearing-price market does when demand outruns cheap supply.

What is genuinely unresolved is who should bear the cost. Right now the answer is largely "everyone on the system, in proportion to their existing usage." Every reform currently in motion is an attempt to change that answer before the next several auctions lock it in.

---

*Figures in this article are drawn from PJM's published Base Residual Auction results, its independent market monitor's public analyses, and filings at FERC and state utility commissions. Auction results and reform proceedings are updated regularly; for the current numbers, consult PJM's posted auction reports and your state commission's docket. Bill impact ranges are estimates and will differ by utility, zone, and service class. This is general information, not investment or legal advice.*
